title: Feature engineering for ranking
summary: Design the numbers a learning-to-rank model sees: per-field BM25, coverage and proximity, freshness and popularity, click and query features, normalization, missing values, and logging features to avoid skew.
outcomes: Classify ranking signals as query, document or query-document features and explain why per-field BM25 beats one whole-document score
Compute per-field BM25, match coverage and a minimum proximity window for a small collection
Explain why heavy-tailed counts need a log or rank transform before z-score or min-max normalization
Choose how to encode missing feature values and explain why query-only features need interactions
Explain train/serve skew and design query-time feature logging that avoids it

lessons.title: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair

blocks.md:
In the BM25 course you scored documents with one formula. Real search engines combine hundreds of signals: how well the title matches, how well the body matches, how popular the page is, how fresh it is, how often people clicked it for this query. A **learning-to-rank** (LTR) model learns how to weigh those signals from labeled examples, the same way any supervised model learns weights by minimizing a loss.

The model never sees the query or the page. It sees a **feature vector**: a fixed list of numbers computed for one (query, document) pair. Everything the model can know has to be encoded in those numbers, so this course is about designing them.

Elasticsearch's LTR documentation sorts features into three families:

- **Document features** depend only on the document (its price, its PageRank, its age).
- **Query features** depend only on the query (for example, the number of words in it).
- **Query-document features** describe the document in the context of the query (for example, the BM25 score of the `title` field).

Yahoo's challenge overview (Chapelle and Chang, 2011) uses the same three-part split and adds finer categories: web graph, document statistics, document classifiers, query, text match, topical matching, click, external references and time.

blocks.title: From a query and a document to a score

scenes.caption: Inputs: a query string and a stored document. The model cannot read either one directly.
Query features need only the query, document features need only the document, and query-document features need both.
All three families are concatenated into one fixed-length vector. MSLR-WEB30K uses 136 numbers per pair; LETOR 4.0 uses 46.
The model maps the vector to a score, and documents are sorted by score.
The same vector is written to a log so training later uses exactly the numbers the model saw. Lesson 5 explains why this matters.

blocks.md: Public LTR datasets show what such vectors look like. **LETOR 4.0** (Qin and Liu) gives 46 features per pair: TF, IDF, TF-IDF, document length, BM25 and three language-model scores, each computed on five *streams* (body, anchor, title, URL, whole document), plus PageRank, inlink and outlink counts, number of slashes in the URL, URL length and number of child pages. **MSLR-WEB30K** from Microsoft has 136 features per pair: the same five-stream text features (BM25 is features 106 to 110) plus PageRank, a quality-classifier score, query-URL click count, URL click count and URL dwell time. MSLR labels run from 0 (irrelevant) to 4 (perfectly relevant).

blocks.prompt: Yahoo's data includes a strong text-match feature, BM25F-SD (BM25 over fields plus proximity). On the Set 1 test split, how much better (in NDCG, a 0 to 1 score of ranking quality) do you expect a gradient-boosted tree model using all 519 features to be than ranking by that single feature?
blocks.reveal: Clearly better, but not overwhelmingly: NDCG 0.790 for GBDT versus 0.732 for BM25F-SD alone, with a linear RankSVM in between at 0.759 (Chapelle and Chang, Table 5). The best single text feature already does most of the work; the other features and a nonlinear model buy the rest. Note also that the authors call BM25F-SD *one of the most predictive features*, so it is a feature in the model, not a competitor to it.

blocks.title: Yahoo LTR Challenge Set 1 test NDCG (Chapelle and Chang 2011)

scenes.caption: A single well-engineered text-match feature reaches NDCG 0.732.
A linear model over all features: 0.759.
Gradient-boosted trees over all features: 0.790. The gains come from combining many signals, not from replacing text match.

blocks.md: Feature engineering is valuable enough that companies guard it. Yahoo released only anonymous feature values, explaining that feature engineering is a critical component of any learning-to-rank system and that releasing queries and URLs would risk reverse engineering of their features.

A ranking model only knows what its feature vector tells it. If a signal that decides relevance (freshness for news, location for local search) is not encoded as a number for each query-document pair, no amount of model tuning can recover it.

blocks.question: A food-delivery search ranks restaurants. Which of these is a query-document feature?
options: The restaurant's average rating
The number of words the user typed
BM25 of the query against the restaurant's menu text
The hour of the day the restaurant opened
blocks.explain: Menu BM25 needs both the query and the restaurant, so it is query-document. Rating and opening hour describe only the restaurant (document features), and word count describes only the query (a query feature).

blocks.question: Why do LETOR and MSLR compute BM25 separately on body, anchor, title and URL instead of once on the whole page?
options: A match in the title and a match in the body are different evidence, and separate features let the model learn a weight for each
BM25 cannot be computed on long documents
It makes the index smaller
Search engines are required to by the TREC rules
blocks.explain: Per-field (per-stream) scores keep the evidence separate. A model can then learn that a title match is worth more than a body match for this collection, which a single whole-document score cannot express.

lessons.title: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity

blocks.md:
Here is a toy collection for the query **fast json parser**. Each of five documents has a short title and a body:

- D1 title *fast json parser*; body: a fast json parser written in rust parses large files with a streaming parser.
- D2 title *json tools*; body: this parser is fast and handles json from many sources so json logs are easy.
- D3 title *fast csv reader*; body: reads csv files fast, there is no json support yet.
- D4 title *parser combinators*; body: build a parser for any grammar including json with small fast functions.
- D5 title *web server*; body: a fast web server with routing and middleware.

**BM25 per field.** Compute BM25 (Lucene form, $k_1 = 1.2$, $b = 0.75$) separately for each field, each with its own statistics: the number of documents containing the term *in that field*, and that field's average length. Titles average 2.4 words; bodies average 11.8.

blocks.caption: Here $n_t$, $|d|$ and avgdl are all measured within one field. The same term gets a different IDF in each field.

blocks.prompt: The word fast appears in every body but in only two titles. What happens to its IDF in each field?
blocks.reveal: In titles, fast occurs in 2 of 5 documents, so its IDF is ln(1 + 3.5/2.5) = 0.875. In bodies it occurs in all 5, so its IDF is ln(1 + 0.5/5.5) = 0.087, ten times smaller. Per-field statistics let the same word be informative in titles and nearly worthless in bodies.

blocks.md:
**Match coverage.** MSLR's first features are *covered query term number* and *covered query term ratio* per stream: how many of the query's terms appear at all. Vespa exposes the same idea as `fieldMatch(name).queryCompleteness` (matched query terms divided by query terms) and `fieldCompleteness` (matched tokens divided by field length). Coverage catches what BM25 can blur: a document can score well by repeating one rare term while missing the others.

**Proximity.** Do the query terms appear close together? A simple version is the smallest window of body tokens that contains every query term. Yahoo's overview lists proximity features (terms closer together count as better evidence), and its BM25F-SD feature adds proximity to BM25F. Vespa provides `nativeProximity` and `fieldMatch(name).proximity`, which is close to 1 when matched terms are close and goes toward 0 as they spread apart.

blocks.title: Smallest body window containing all three query terms

scenes.caption: Three bodies that contain all three terms (truncated to 6 characters per cell). Window = last position minus first position plus 1.
D1: fast, json, parser at positions 1 to 3. Window 3, the tightest possible.
D2: parser at 1, fast at 3, json at 6. Window 6. The terms are present but spread over a clause.
D4: parser at 2, json at 7, fast at 10. Window 9: these words are about different things in the sentence.
Body BM25 barely separates D2 (0.42) and D4 (0.41). The window (6 versus 9) does: proximity adds information BM25 throws away by treating text as a bag of words.

blocks.md: Put the features side by side. Proximity is encoded as 1 / window so that larger means better; D3 and D5 lack a query term in the body, so their window does not exist. They get 0 here, which is itself a design choice (lesson 4).

blocks.title: Query-document features for the query fast json parser

scenes.caption: Six features per pair, all computed by the script for this toy collection.
Whole-document BM25 (title and body concatenated) ranks D4 (0.51) above D2 (0.46). Merged statistics wash out the title signal.
Per-field BM25 keeps them apart: D1 dominates the title column with 1.08, and D2 ties D4 on title (0.43) but they differ elsewhere.
Coverage: D3 matches only 2 of 3 terms in its body (0.67) and D5 only 1 (0.33). That is missing-term evidence that BM25 sums hide.
Proximity separates the near-tie between D2 and D4. A model can now learn how much each column matters from labels.

blocks.md: Per-field BM25 features are not BM25F. BM25F (the subject of Elasticsearch's `combined_fields` query) merges term frequencies across fields before saturating. Separate per-field features saturate each field on its own and let the model weigh them. Both are useful; they are different numbers.

Features are cheap to add and expensive to compute at scale. Engines therefore rank in phases: a cheap first phase over all matches (Vespa describes `nativeRank` as a good first-phase function, and `bm25` as cheaper still), then expensive features and the learned model on only the top results.

blocks.question: Document X has the query terms in its body at positions 4, 5 and 6. Document Y has them at positions 2, 40 and 77. Their body BM25 scores are equal. Which feature tells them apart?
options: Body BM25 with a larger k1
Body coverage ratio
Body length
Minimum window (proximity)
blocks.explain: Both contain all terms, so coverage is 1.0 for both, and BM25 ignores positions entirely. Only a positional feature such as the minimum covering window (3 versus 76) separates them.

blocks.question: You compute title BM25 for one document using IDF from the body field because it is already cached. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, IDF is a property of the term
Terms that are common in bodies but rare in titles get far too little weight in the title feature
The score becomes negative
Coverage stops working
blocks.explain: IDF depends on the field's own document frequencies. In the toy, fast has IDF 0.875 in titles but 0.087 in bodies. Using body IDF would make a title match on fast look almost worthless.

lessons.title: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks

blocks.md: **Document features** are computed once per document and reused for every query: quality-classifier scores (MSLR feature 132), PageRank and inlinks (web graph), URL length and slash count (document statistics), popularity and age. Their raw values are often badly shaped for learning, so they are usually transformed before use.

**Freshness.** Raw age in seconds is not what you want: the difference between 1 and 8 days old matters for news, the difference between 300 and 307 days rarely does. Vespa's rank features show two shapes. Linear `freshness(name)` is $\max(1 - \text{age}/\text{maxAge}, 0)$, with maxAge defaulting to 90 days. `freshness(name).logscale` also goes from 1 to 0 but drops quickly at first; it is tuned so that age = halfResponse (default 7 days) gives exactly 0.5.

blocks.caption: Vespa's logscale freshness, written with h = halfResponse. With the defaults (90 days, 7 days), s = 49/76 = 0.645 days.

curves.label: logscale
curves.expr: max((ln(maxAge + h^2/(maxAge-2*h)) - ln(min(x,maxAge) + h^2/(maxAge-2*h))) / (ln(maxAge + h^2/(maxAge-2*h)) - ln(h^2/(maxAge-2*h))), 0)

scenes.caption: Defaults. At 7 days logscale is 0.5 while linear is still 0.922; at 30 days they are 0.219 versus 0.667. Logscale spends its range on the first week.
halfResponse = 1 day: a breaking-news profile where yesterday is already half as fresh.
maxAge = 180 days: linear freshness now separates documents up to six months old.

blocks.md: **Popularity.** Counts such as views, clicks or inlinks are heavy-tailed: a few documents have orders of magnitude more than the rest. Our five toy documents have views 12, 340, 95000, 50 and 2100. Taking $\ln(1 + v)$ turns them into 2.56, 5.83, 11.46, 3.93 and 7.65, so for counts well above 1 a ratio of 10 becomes a difference of about 2.3. Yahoo notes another standard fix: normalize counts by exposure, for example click-through rate (clicks divided by impressions) instead of raw clicks.

blocks.title: Popularity feature: raw views versus ln(1 + views)

scenes.caption: Raw views. D3 has 95000 and everything else looks like zero next to it.
ln(1 + views): 2.56, 5.83, 11.46, 3.93, 7.65. The ordering is unchanged, but the gaps between ordinary documents are now visible.

blocks.md: **Click features** come from user behavior: click probability, first click, last click, long-dwell click, skip rate (Yahoo's list), and MSLR's query-URL click count and dwell time. They are among the strongest signals, but they are biased by position. In Joachims et al.'s 2005 eye-tracking study, users in the swapped condition saw Google's top two results in reversed order. When the second-shown abstract was judged *more* relevant, users still clicked only the first link 10 times versus only the second link 7 times. The authors call this **trust bias**: users click what is on top partly because it is on top.

blocks.title: Swapped order, link 2 more relevant (Joachims et al. 2005, Table 3)

scenes.caption: 36 result pages where the second-shown abstract was judged more relevant than the first.
Users still clicked only the less relevant top link more often (10) than only the more relevant second link (7). A raw click-count feature inherits this position effect.

blocks.md: A raw click count rewards documents for having been ranked high in the past, which feeds back into ranking them high again. Correcting this (for example the propensity weighting of Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel 2017) is a topic of its own; at minimum, normalize clicks by impressions and record the position each impression was shown at.

**Query features** are things like the number of query terms (Vespa's `queryTermCount`), query frequency and query click-through rate. Yahoo also describes **result-set** features: averages of other features over the top documents, such as the average adult score of the results as a signal that the query itself is adult.

blocks.prompt: A ranking model scores each document as $w \cdot x$ (a linear model). You add the feature query term count. Can this feature ever change the order of documents within one query?
blocks.reveal: No. Every document for the same query gets the same value, so the linear model adds the same constant $w \cdot c$ to all of them and the order is unchanged. A query feature helps only through **interactions**: a tree model can split on it first (short queries use one sub-ranker, long queries another), or you can cross it with a query-document feature by hand.

blocks.md: **Interaction features** combine signals explicitly: title coverage times a flag for single-word queries, freshness times a query is time-sensitive score, or a document's BM25 divided by the best BM25 in the result list. Trees learn some interactions on their own; linear models need them built by hand.
Shape raw signals before the model sees them: turn age into a decaying freshness, counts into logs or rates, and remember that query-only features can only matter through interactions.

blocks.question: A news ranker uses linear freshness with maxAge 90 days. Editors complain that a 2-hour-old story and a 2-day-old story look the same to the model. What change best fixes this?
options: Use a logscale freshness with a small halfResponse such as 1 day
Increase maxAge to 365 days
Drop freshness and rely on popularity
Use raw age in seconds without transformation
blocks.explain: Linear freshness drops only 1/90 per day, so 2 hours and 2 days differ by about 0.02. A logscale curve with halfResponse 1 day spends most of its range in the first days. Raising maxAge makes the slope even flatter.

blocks.question: Which feature is most likely to be inflated by position bias?
options: Title BM25
Query-URL click count
URL length
Document age
blocks.explain: Click counts depend on where the document was shown: top results get examined and clicked more even when a lower result is more relevant, as the swapped-order experiment showed. The other three do not depend on past rankings.

blocks.md: Features live on wildly different scales: coverage is between 0 and 1, title BM25 here reaches 1.08, views reach 95000. **Normalization** maps each feature to a common range. The Elasticsearch LTR plugin supports two normalizers and says that some models, especially linear ones like SVMRank, rely on normalization to work correctly. Solr's LTR module offers the same pair (MinMaxNormalizer with min and max, StandardNormalizer with avg and std) plus an IdentityNormalizer.

blocks.caption: Standard (z-score) normalization: the mean maps to 0 and one standard deviation to plus or minus 1. Min-max: the minimum maps to 0 and the maximum to 1.

blocks.prompt: Apply z-score normalization to raw views (12, 340, 95000, 50, 2100). Will the result make the four ordinary documents easy to tell apart?
blocks.reveal: No. The mean is 19500.4 and the standard deviation is 37757.65, both driven by the single outlier. The z-scores are -0.52, -0.51, 2.00, -0.52, -0.46: four documents are squeezed within 0.06 of each other. Normalization rescales; it does not fix a skewed shape. Apply ln(1 + x) first and the z-scores become -1.20, -0.15, 1.67, -0.76, 0.44.

blocks.title: Five ways to encode the same popularity values

scenes.caption: Raw views for D1 to D5.
z-score of raw values: -0.52, -0.51, 2.00, -0.52, -0.46. The outlier eats the scale.
Min-max of raw values: 0, 0.003, 1, 0.0004, 0.022 (shown rounded). Same problem, squeezed into [0, 1].
ln(1 + x), then z-score: -1.20, -0.15, 1.67, -0.76, 0.44. Ordinary documents now spread out.

Rank transform (Yahoo's choice): the number of values strictly smaller, divided by n minus 1. Result: 0, 0.5, 1, 0.25, 0.75. Immune to outliers, but equal spacing hides how far apart values really are.

blocks.md: Yahoo normalized all 700 challenge features to [0, 1] with exactly that rank transform (an empirical cumulative distribution), computed jointly over the training, validation and test data. LETOR 4.0 instead ships a **QueryLevelNorm** version that normalizes each feature within the documents of a single query, which is why its sample rows are full of values like 0.000000 and 1.000000.

blocks.title: Best title BM25 per query, raw versus query-level min-max

scenes.caption: Raw best title BM25 in the toy collection: 1.35 for web server, 1.08 for fast json parser, only 0.43 for json (no title is just json).
After per-query min-max, the best document for every query becomes 1.0. Scores are comparable across queries, but the model can no longer see that the best json match is weak.

blocks.md: Tree models (gradient-boosted decision trees, the model family Elasticsearch's built-in LTR runs, for example LambdaMART trained with XGBoost) split on thresholds, so any global monotone transform of a feature (log, z-score, min-max with fixed constants) leaves the learned splits equivalent. Per-query normalization is different: it changes which documents share a value, so it changes what even a tree can learn.

**Missing values.** Some features do not exist for some pairs: the proximity window when a term is absent, a language-model score when no query term matches, an attribute that was never set. Real systems handle this explicitly:

- LETOR 4.0's NULL version marks missing language-model features as NULL (they would be minus infinity); its MIN version replaces NULL with the feature's minimum within the same query.
- Yahoo sets a feature that is undefined for a dataset to 0.
- The Elasticsearch LTR plugin's `missing_as_zero` option logs 0 when a feature query does not match.
- Vespa's `attribute(name)` returns NaN if not set and warns that undefined values lead to undefined behavior in ranking expressions; check with `isNan()`.

Filling a missing value with 0 is safe only when 0 already means the worst value. For a feature like 1/window it does. For a z-scored feature, 0 means average, so a missing value silently becomes an average document. Use the worst observed value (LETOR's MIN approach) or add a separate is-missing flag.

blocks.question: You fit min-max normalization on last month's training data (views max 95000). Today a document has 400000 views. What does the serving-time normalizer produce, and is that a problem?
options: Exactly 1.0, nothing to worry about
An error, because the value is out of range
0, because unknown values default to zero
About 4.2, outside the range the model was trained on
blocks.explain: Min-max uses the stored constants: (400000 - 12) / (95000 - 12) is about 4.2. A linear model extrapolates past anything it saw; a tree treats it like the largest training value. Clipping, log transforms or rank-based encodings make this less surprising.

blocks.question: A z-scored feature has missing values filled with 0. What does the model effectively believe about those documents?
options: That they are the worst on this feature
That they are exactly average on this feature
That the feature is unknown
Nothing, zeros are ignored
blocks.explain: After z-scoring, 0 is the mean. Filling with 0 claims the document is average, which may be wildly optimistic (or pessimistic). Fill with a deliberate value and add an is-missing indicator if absence carries information.

blocks.question: Which normalization lets the model compare match strength across queries, so it can tell that the best json match is weak?
options: A global transform with fixed constants, such as min-max fitted on the whole training set
Per-query min-max (LETOR QueryLevelNorm)
Both preserve it equally
Neither, BM25 cannot be compared across documents
blocks.explain: A global transform applies the same constants to every query, so a raw 0.43 stays lower than a raw 1.08. Per-query min-max maps every query's best document to 1, erasing that difference.

lessons.title: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve

blocks.md:
Training data for LTR is a **judgment list** (graded labels for query-document pairs, from editors or derived from clicks) joined with a feature vector for each pair. The tempting shortcut is to compute features later, offline, when you assemble training data. That breaks whenever the feature at training time differs from the feature the model will see at serving time. This mismatch is called **train/serve skew**.

The Elasticsearch LTR plugin's guidance is direct: you want the exact value of a feature at the precise time a user interaction happened. OpenSearch's LTR docs say the same and note that a local copy of the index may be slightly out of sync with the live index.

blocks.prompt: Our toy index grows by five documents titled json schema notes. Nothing about D1 or D2 changed. Recompute their title BM25 for fast json parser: what happens?
blocks.reveal: Both move. N goes from 5 to 10 and json now appears in 7 titles, so json's title IDF falls from 0.875 to 0.383 while fast and parser become relatively rarer (0.875 to 1.482). Average title length goes from 2.4 to 2.7. D1 rises from 1.08 to 1.45 and D2 falls from 0.43 to 0.19. If D2 was labeled from a click last week, the recomputed feature is not the one the user saw ranked.

blocks.title: Title BM25 logged at query time versus recomputed after the index grew

scenes.caption: Logged when the user searched (5 documents in the index).
Recomputed a week later against 10 documents. The gap between D1 and D2 widened from 2.5x to 7.5x, though neither document changed.

blocks.md:
Other common sources of skew:

- **Time-relative features.** Freshness computed at training time (weeks later) is much lower than it was when the user saw the result.
- **Counters that include the outcome.** A popularity feature recomputed after the fact already counts the very click you are trying to predict.
- **Two implementations.** An offline Python pipeline that tokenizes differently from the search engine produces different BM25 values for the same pair.

scenes.caption: The query arrives. The service issues a search that runs the feature set (an sltr query) for the top results.
The engine returns results with each document's feature vector attached, exactly the values used for ranking.
The service logs the impression: query, document ids, positions shown and feature vectors.
Later the user's clicks are logged and joined to the impression by an id.
The trainer reads labels joined with the logged features. Nothing is recomputed, so training sees what serving saw.

blocks.md: In the Elasticsearch LTR plugin, a **feature set** is a named group of features used for logging and model evaluation; each feature is a Mustache-templated query whose parameters (here `keywords`) are filled in at search time. To log, you add an `sltr` query with a `_name` and an `ltr_log` extension that points at that name; you place it in a bool filter clause so it does not change scores. In production the same mechanism logs from the `sltr` query that runs the model. Solr's LTR module logs through the `[features]` document transformer (for example `fl=id,score,[features]`) and passes query-time inputs as external feature information, such as `efi.text`.

blocks.caption: Elasticsearch LTR plugin: define a feature set with one templated feature, then log its values for chosen documents (adapted from the plugin documentation).

blocks.md: Features used for training must be produced by the same code, against the same index state and at the same moment as the features used for serving. Log the vector at query time; do not reconstruct it later.

Store normalization constants with the model, not in a separate preprocessing script. The Elasticsearch LTR plugin puts `feature_normalizers` (for example standard with mean 1970 and standard_deviation 30 for a release year) in the model definition, so serving applies the same transform training used.

blocks.question: A team logs only document ids and query strings, then recomputes all features nightly for training. Which feature is most at risk of skew?
options: URL length
Number of query terms
Freshness computed from age relative to now
Whether the title contains a query term
blocks.explain: URL length, query term count and title containment are stable for a fixed document and query. Freshness relative to now is recomputed hours or days later, so every training example looks older than it was when the user saw it.

blocks.question: Offline NDCG of the new model is excellent, but online it underperforms the old one. Features were computed by a Python script for training and by the search engine for serving. What is the first thing to check?
options: Whether the learning rate was too high
Whether NDCG is the right metric
Whether the model has too few trees
Whether the two pipelines produce identical feature values for the same query-document pairs
blocks.explain: Train/serve skew is the prime suspect when offline and online disagree. Log the engine's feature vectors for a sample of pairs and diff them against the script's values. Fixing the model cannot help if its inputs differ.
